faq.a: Yes; up to 10 % present without skin involvement, so treat based on respiratory or circulatory signs.
faq.q: Can anaphylaxis occur without a rash?

faq.a: IM provides rapid absorption with lower risk of arrhythmia; IV is reserved for refractory shock under cardiac monitoring.
faq.q: Why is adrenaline given intramuscularly, not intravenously?

exam: A 22‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden wheeze and hypotension after a bee sting – what is your immediate management and why? — Give IM adrenaline, high‑flow O₂, IV fluids; explain adrenaline’s actions on airway, vasculature, and heart.

How would you differentiate anaphylaxis from acute severe asthma in a patient with wheeze and no rash? — Look for skin or GI symptoms, hypotension, and rapid onset after exposure; asthma lacks systemic signs.

A patient on penicillin develops urticaria and mild hypotension; why is epinephrine preferred over antihistamines as first‑line? — Antihistamines relieve itching but do not reverse airway edema or vasodilation; epinephrine addresses life‑threatening physiology.
In a low‑resource clinic without serum tryptase, how do you confirm anaphylaxis? — Rely on clinical criteria: exposure, rapid multisystem involvement, and response to adrenaline.

What are the contraindications to using high‑dose corticosteroids in acute allergic reactions? — None for anaphylaxis; avoid delaying adrenaline; be aware of infection risk in immunocompromised patients.

A child receives an intramuscular adrenaline dose but remains hypotensive; what are the next steps? — Repeat IM dose after 5 min, start IV crystalloid bolus, consider IV adrenaline infusion if monitored.

Explain why a patient with known sickle cell disease may have a more severe reaction to a malaria drug allergy. — Baseline endothelial dysfunction and chronic inflammation increase risk of shock; careful monitoring is required.

What follow‑up plan would you give a patient discharged after a moderate reaction to a herbal remedy? — Advise avoidance, prescribe an adrenaline auto‑injector if possible, arrange allergy testing, and provide written emergency action plan.
ai.title: Acute Allergic Reactions
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute allergic reactions are rapid hypersensitivity responses that can progress to life‑threatening anaphylaxis. Prompt recognition, severity grading, and targeted treatment are essential, especially where resources are limited.

b: Diagnosis is clinical: exposure history, rapid symptom onset, and involvement of skin, respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal systems.
sections.p: An acute allergic reaction is a sudden onset (usually ≤4 h) immune‑mediated response to an allergen, ranging from localized urticaria to systemic anaphylaxis.

b: Mild: limited urticaria, itching.
Moderate: wheeze, abdominal pain, vomiting, or angio‑edema without airway obstruction.
Severe: stridor, hypoxia, hypotension, loss of consciousness.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the World Allergy Organization (WAO) system: mild (skin only), moderate (skin plus respiratory or GI symptoms), severe (airway compromise, hypotension, or shock).

b: Insect venom (bees, wasps, ants)
Food allergens (peanuts, shellfish, milk)
Beta‑lactam antibiotics
Sulfonamide drugs
Herbal remedies containing unknown botanicals
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the most common triggers are insect stings, foods (peanuts, shellfish), drugs (penicillins, sulfonamides), and traditional herbal preparations.

b: Skin: urticaria, angio‑edema, flushing
Respiratory: wheeze, stridor, dyspnoea
Cardiovascular: tachycardia, hypotension, syncope
GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
sections.p: Patients develop sudden itching, flushing, or hives, followed by possible swelling of lips/eyes, wheezing, abdominal cramps, or collapse.
Investigations support severity assessment; many may be unavailable, so rely on bedside findings.

t.b: Is there hypoxia? – SpO₂ < 94 % indicates need for supplemental O₂ and possible airway support.
Is the patient hypotensive? – Systolic < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg signals severe reaction.
Was anaphylaxis present? – Levels > 11.4 µg/L within 1–2 h support mast‑cell activation.
Is there renal or electrolyte disturbance from shock? – Look for rising creatinine or metabolic acidosis.

b: Stridor or inability to speak
Rapidly falling blood pressure
Altered mental status
Persistent tachycardia > 120 bpm despite fluids
sections.p: Rapid progression to airway obstruction or circulatory collapse demands immediate emergency care.

b: High‑flow O₂ via mask – maintain SpO₂ ≥ 94 %.
IV crystalloid bolus 20 mL/kg if hypotensive – restores intravascular volume.
H1‑antihistamine (e.g., chlorpheniramine) – relieves cutaneous symptoms; avoid sedating antihistamines if airway at risk.
Observe for at least 4 h after symptom resolution; longer if severe.
sections.p: First step is to secure the airway, then give intramuscular adrenaline, followed by supportive measures and identification of the trigger.

b: Prescribe an adrenaline auto‑injector if available; teach self‑administration.
Referral to allergy clinic for skin‑prick or specific IgE testing when feasible.
Avoid known triggers; wear medical alert identification.
Review all recent medications and herbal products.
sections.p: Patients need allergen identification, education, and an emergency action plan.

b: Vasovagal syncope – prodrome of light‑headedness without skin changes.
Acute asthma exacerbation – wheeze without urticaria or angio‑edema.
Septic shock – fever, purulent source, and gradual onset.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic acute allergic reactions must be distinguished to avoid mis‑management.

b: Normal blood pressure early in anaphylaxis – can fall rapidly; repeat measurements.
Absence of skin signs – up to 10 % of anaphylaxis present without cutaneous involvement.
sections.p: Certain bedside findings may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg
